newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe industry urges action on deficit.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe industry urges action on deficit.

text.p: The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) urged the government on Tuesday to act urgently to narrow its burgeoning budget deficit, seen stunting economic growth.

CZI president Jonee Blanchfield told Reuters ahead of the CZI's annual congress starting on Wednesday that the government risked rolling back gains made under Western donor-backed economic reforms started in 1991 if it continued failing to cut down on the deficit.

"We have been through the processes of removing controls but economic growth is not sufficiently satisfactory, standards of living are not improving, the budget deficit is just too high," Blanchfield said.
Zimbabwe's budget deficit is expected to widen to 11 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the financial year ended June 30, off a target of 8.5 percent.

President Robert Mugabe's government consistently missed targets to slice the budget deficit to five percent of GDP by the end of the first phase of its economic structural adjustment programme in 1995.

In September 1995, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, which marshalled Western donor aid for the southern African country, suspended crucial balance of payments support as targets were missed again.
The two organisations say they are now looking to the country's budget for the new financial year to December 31, 1998 which is scheduled for July 24 before deciding when to resume aid.

"I don't think we can fool around any more. The government cannot continue to try and finance the deficit from ridiculous levies which are creating hardships and borrowing from the domestic market which denies the private sector the money that's needed for expansion," Blanchfield said.
She said the government needed to forge ahead faster with privatisation of loss-making state firms seen draining public money and improve tax collection.
She added that captains of Zimbabwean industries would try, at their annual congress starting on Wednesday, to impress on the government the need for urgent action on these and other issues.

"One of the worst things which is a time bomb is unemployment. Employment creation is not happening. If we continue not giving our young people jobs we are going to be in real trouble," Blanchfield said.
Unemployment in the official sector is about 50 percent, with the country producing an army of 200,000 school-leavers annually to chase only 70,000 jobs that are created.
